```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(viridis)
library(mgcv)
library(broom)

# Domain packages, used in the two "in practice" slides near the end.
# install.packages(c("vowels", "phonR", "quanteda", "tidytext"))
library(vowels)
library(phonR)
library(quanteda)
library(tidytext)

# Datasets shipped with the packages; library() does not attach them.
data(ohiovowels, package = "vowels")
data(data_corpus_inaugural, package = "quanteda")

systemfonts::register_font(
  "Albert Sans",
  plain  = "../../stylesheets/fonts/AlbertSans-400.ttf",
  bold   = "../../stylesheets/fonts/AlbertSans-700.ttf",
  italic = "../../stylesheets/fonts/AlbertSans-400.ttf"
)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png", dev.args = list(bg = "white"))

# Simulated prominence data: F0 peak and duration per trial, with speaker,
# item, condition, and speech rate. See scripts/make-prominence-data.R.
prominence <- read.csv("data/prominence_trials.csv") |>
  mutate(
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("plain", "focus", "contrast")),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("f", "m"), labels = c("female", "male"))
  )

uzk_blue      <- "#005176"
uzk_turquoise <- "#009dcc"
uzk_coral     <- "#ea564f"
uzk_muted     <- "#547685"

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Albert Sans", base_size = 15) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.05)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = uzk_muted),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
)
```

## Overview {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### What this deck adds

The first two decks teach the grammar and the machinery. This one covers the **data shapes of prominence research**:

1. **Contours and spaces** — F0 over time, vowel formants
2. **Individuals** — speaker and item effects, not only means
3. **Ordinal, proportion, and count data** — ratings, accuracy, corpora
4. **Models and data care** — coefficient plots, posteriors, fonts, disclosure, missing data

### Plan

- **Contours and spaces:** 20 min
- **Individuals:** 10 min
- **Ratings and counts:** 20 min
- **Models and data care:** 20 min

*Total: 70 minutes.*
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### Relationship to the other decks

[`slides.qmd`](slides.html) covers the grammar and integrity; [`slides-advanced.qmd`](slides-advanced.html) covers scales, models, and publication. Everything here assumes those two.
:::

**Examples:** simulated data, marked as such in each subtitle, plus `data/prominence_trials.csv` for the coefficient plot.

**Prerequisites:** the basic workshop or equivalent experience with `ggplot2`.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This is a domain appendix, not a replacement. The examples are simulated so that the intended pattern is visible; the code runs unchanged on real data. Emphasise that the plotting grammar stays the same — what changes is the shape of the data (time within trial, formants per token, ordinal responses) and the figures that answer those questions.
:::

## Part I: Contours and spaces {.center}

### After this part: plot a trajectory without lying

---

## F0 contours over time {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-contours
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of simulated F0 contours for 12 speakers, accented and unaccented. Left: every speaker's contour as a thin line, showing a peak around the middle for accented items. Right: the mean contour per condition with a 95 percent confidence band."
set.seed(1252)
contour_times <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 21)
contour_speakers <- factor(sprintf("S%02d", 1:12))
speaker_offset <- rnorm(12, 0, 10)

sim_contours <- expand.grid(
  speaker = contour_speakers,
  condition = c("unaccented", "accented"),
  time = contour_times
) |>
  mutate(
    s = as.integer(speaker),
    f0 = 115 + speaker_offset[s] +
      ifelse(condition == "accented", 18, 0) *
        exp(-((time - 0.5)^2) / (2 * 0.13^2)) +
      rnorm(n(), 0, 3)
  )

contour_means <- sim_contours |>
  group_by(condition, time) |>
  summarise(m = mean(f0), se = sd(f0) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se)

condition_cols <- c(unaccented = uzk_muted, accented = uzk_coral)

p_all <- ggplot(
  sim_contours,
  aes(time, f0, colour = condition, group = interaction(speaker, condition))
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = condition_cols) +
  labs(title = "Every speaker", x = "Normalised time", y = "F0 (Hz)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_mean <- ggplot(contour_means, aes(time, m, colour = condition, fill = condition)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = condition_cols) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = condition_cols) +
  labs(title = "Mean ± 95% CI", x = "Normalised time", y = NULL)

p_all | p_mean
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Normalise time** per token before averaging; raw milliseconds are not comparable across segments.
- Draw **every speaker** thin and the summary thick; a bar of means hides the trajectories.
- The band is a CI for the **mean contour**, not for a new speaker.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Facet by condition or colour by it, but keep the same y scale.
- Say whether the contour is raw, z-scored per speaker, or in semitones.
- Simulated here; the code is identical on real tracks.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Point at the peak in the accented condition around the middle of the window. The left panel shows that the peak is consistent across speakers but the levels differ; the right panel shows the summary. The common mistake is a bar chart of mean F0 per condition, which discards the trajectory entirely.
:::

## Difference curves {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-difference
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "A difference curve over normalised time: the mean difference in F0 between accented and unaccented items, with a 95 percent confidence band, rising from zero to about 18 Hz in the middle and returning to zero. A dashed line marks zero."
diff_curves <- sim_contours |>
  select(speaker, condition, time, f0) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = f0) |>
  mutate(diff = accented - unaccented) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(m = mean(diff), se = sd(diff) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se)

ggplot(diff_curves, aes(time, m)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = uzk_coral, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  labs(title = "Difference curve: accented − unaccented",
       subtitle = "simulated data; where the band leaves zero, the contrast is there",
       x = "Normalised time", y = "Difference in F0 (Hz)")
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- A difference curve answers **where** an effect lives, not only whether it exists.
- The zero line is the null; the band is the uncertainty about the mean difference.
- Normalise time first, then subtract within speaker and item.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- In papers, add a horizontal bar marking the window used for analysis.
- Prefer this to two separate mean plots whose scales invite misreading.
- The same recipe works for ERP amplitudes, gaze proportions, and intensity.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This is the figure reviewers ask for when the claim is "the peak is delayed". Two condition means can look different without telling you where; the difference curve with its band does. Mention that the band narrows because the differences are paired within speaker.
:::

## Vowel spaces {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-vowels
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "A simulated vowel space with F2 on the reversed x-axis and F1 on the reversed y-axis. Six vowels are shown as clouds of points with 68 percent ellipses: high vowels i and u at the top, open vowels at the bottom, front vowels to the right."
set.seed(1252)
vowel_centres <- data.frame(
  vowel = c("i", "ɪ", "ɛ", "æ", "ɑ", "u"),
  F1 = c(280, 400, 550, 700, 750, 320),
  F2 = c(2300, 2000, 1900, 1700, 1100, 900)
)
speaker_f1 <- rnorm(8, 0, 25)
speaker_f2 <- rnorm(8, 0, 70)

sim_vowels <- expand.grid(
  speaker = factor(1:8),
  vowel = vowel_centres$vowel,
  token = 1:25
) |>
  left_join(vowel_centres, by = "vowel") |>
  mutate(
    s = as.integer(speaker),
    F1 = F1 + speaker_f1[s] + rnorm(n(), 0, 30),
    F2 = F2 + speaker_f2[s] + rnorm(n(), 0, 80)
  )

ggplot(sim_vowels, aes(F2, F1, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(title = "Vowel space", subtitle = "simulated tokens; axes reversed, as in the vowel chart",
       x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = "Vowel")
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Reverse the axes** (`scale_x_reverse()`, `scale_y_reverse()`): the chart convention is high vowels at the top, front vowels at the right.
- **Normalise before plotting** across speakers (Lobanov or a speaker-specific scaling), or the clouds separate by speaker rather than by vowel.
- Ellipses show spread; points show the tokens. Do not plot centroids only.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- The axes are **Hz, not a metric space**; distances are not comparable across the two dimensions.
- Facet by speaker when individual differences are the question.
- For trajectories (diphthongs), draw the path per token with time as a gradient.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The reversed axes are the first thing reviewers notice. The second is normalisation: without it, a figure of raw Hz mostly shows who has a longer vocal tract. Ask the room which speakers sit high or low, and whether that is vowel quality or speaker size. Mention `scale_x_reverse()` and `stat_ellipse(level = 0.68)`.
:::

## Speaker and item effects {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-individuals
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Two caterpillar plots of simulated effects. Left: the focus-minus-plain F0 difference for each of 20 speakers with 95 percent confidence intervals, ordered by size, ranging from about minus 2 to plus 27 Hz, with two intervals crossing zero. Right: the same for 20 items, ranging from about 2 to 24 Hz, with three intervals crossing zero."
set.seed(1252)
speaker_effect <- rnorm(20, 8, 6)
item_effect <- rnorm(20, 0, 6)
sim_trials <- expand.grid(
  speaker = factor(sprintf("S%02d", 1:20)),
  item = factor(sprintf("I%02d", 1:20)),
  condition = c("plain", "focus")
) |>
  mutate(
    s = as.integer(speaker),
    i = as.integer(item),
    f0 = 120 + rnorm(20, 0, 12)[s] + rnorm(20, 0, 6)[i] +
      (speaker_effect[s] + item_effect[i]) * (condition == "focus") +
      rnorm(n(), 0, 5)
  )

speaker_effects <- sim_trials |>
  select(speaker, item, condition, f0) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = f0) |>
  mutate(diff = focus - plain) |>
  group_by(speaker) |>
  summarise(m = mean(diff), se = sd(diff) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se)

item_effects <- sim_trials |>
  select(speaker, item, condition, f0) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = f0) |>
  mutate(diff = focus - plain) |>
  group_by(item) |>
  summarise(m = mean(diff), se = sd(diff) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se)

p_speakers <- ggplot(speaker_effects, aes(m, reorder(speaker, m))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = uzk_blue, size = 0.35) +
  labs(title = "Speakers", subtitle = "n = 20", x = "Focus − plain (Hz)", y = NULL)

p_items <- ggplot(item_effects, aes(m, reorder(item, m))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = uzk_turquoise, size = 0.35) +
  labs(title = "Items", subtitle = "n = 20", x = "Focus − plain (Hz)", y = NULL)

p_speakers | p_items
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- A mean ± SE collapses **two** variance sources: who was measured (speakers) and what was measured (items).
- Caterpillar plots show both: order by size, show the interval, keep the zero line.
- The same layout works for random effects from `lme4` or posterior draws from `brms`.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- If the effect is consistent for speakers but not items, the generalisation is about speakers, not words.
- Show the raw per-unit estimates before the model; the model is a summary, not a substitute.
- Facet by condition when there are more than two.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Simulated: speaker effects vary around 8 Hz with SD 6; item effects vary around 0 Hz with SD 6, so the item panel is centred on zero and three of its intervals cross it. The figure makes the difference between "the effect exists" and "the effect is general" visible: a focus effect that holds for speakers but not for words generalises to speakers, not to the lexicon. This is the visual counterpart of random slopes and by-unit variability; it also prepares the reader for a mixed model.
:::

## Part III: Ratings and counts {.center}

### After this part: plot the distribution, not only the mean

---

## Ordinal ratings {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-ratings
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bars of simulated acceptability ratings, 1 to 7, for four constructions. Each bar is the share of ratings per construction, coloured from red for 1 at the bottom to blue for 7 at the top; construction A is concentrated at 5 to 7, construction D spreads across 1 to 5."
set.seed(1252)
condition_means <- c(A = 5.6, B = 4.9, C = 4.0, D = 3.2)
sim_ratings <- expand.grid(
  construction = names(condition_means),
  rater = factor(1:40),
  item = 1:12
) |>
  mutate(
    r = as.integer(rater),
    latent = condition_means[construction] +
      rnorm(40, 0, 0.7)[r] + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.9),
    rating = pmin(7, pmax(1, round(latent)))
  )

rating_props <- sim_ratings |>
  count(construction, rating) |>
  group_by(construction) |>
  mutate(p = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(rating_props, aes(construction, p, fill = factor(rating, levels = 7:1))) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, breaks = 1:7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Ratings, not means", subtitle = "simulated; 1 = unacceptable, 7 = fully acceptable",
       x = NULL, y = "Share of ratings", fill = "Rating")
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- A mean of 4.0 can come from "everyone is neutral" or "half love it, half hate it". The stacked distribution separates them.
- Keep the ordinal scale; do not treat 1–7 as interval data in the figure.
- A diverging palette centred on the neutral category makes the direction visible.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- For models, ordinal regression gives predicted **probabilities** per category; plot those rather than a single mean.
- Report the number of raters and items; the share is only as stable as the sample.
- A stacked bar and a density of ratings tell the same story; choose one and label it.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The simulated means differ by less than the spread: C is centred at 4 and D at 3.2, but the bars show that D has more mass at 2 and 3 while C still has support at 5. This is the argument against mean ± SE ratings. Mention that neutral categories should be visually central for diverging scales.
:::

## Proportions with honest intervals {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-proportions
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Four simulated accuracy proportions with two confidence intervals each. Wald intervals (coral) extend past the 100 percent boundary for the higher proportions; Wilson intervals (turquoise) stay inside the bounds and are asymmetric near the edges."
set.seed(1252)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
prop_data <- tibble(
  condition = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  n = 20,
  true_p = c(0.95, 0.90, 0.80, 0.60),
  hits = c(19, 18, 16, 12)
) |>
  mutate(p = hits / n) |>
  mutate(
    wald_lo = p - z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n),
    wald_hi = p + z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n),
    denom = 1 + z^2 / n,
    centre = (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / denom,
    half = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / denom,
    wilson_lo = centre - half,
    wilson_hi = centre + half
  ) |>
  select(condition, p, wald_lo, wald_hi, wilson_lo, wilson_hi) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(condition, p), names_to = c("method", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(wald|wilson)_(lo|hi)")

ggplot(prop_data, aes(p, condition, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = Inf, label = "100%", vjust = 1.6, hjust = -0.1,
           size = 3.2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.45), size = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(wald = uzk_coral, wilson = uzk_turquoise)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.1), labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Two intervals for the same proportion",
       subtitle = "simulated; Wald (asymptotic) runs past 100%, Wilson does not",
       x = "Proportion", y = NULL, colour = "Method")
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Proportions are bounded; the Wald interval is not. Near 0 or 1 it can cross the boundary and collapse to zero width.
- **Wilson** (or Clopper–Pearson) intervals stay inside and are asymmetric where they should be.
- A logit axis (`scale_y_continuous(trans = "logit")`) spreads the ends; name the scale.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- Report *n* per cell; an interval on 5 trials is mostly the prior, not the data.
- For repeated measures, the interval must respect the design (see the intervals slide in the advanced deck).
- Same advice for accuracy, agreement rates, and proportions of annotated categories.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The Wald interval for p = 0.95 with n = 20 runs above 1, which the figure shows. Wilson is the practical default; Clopper–Pearson is more conservative. The point is not the formula but that a bounded quantity needs a bounded interval.
:::

## Corpus counts {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-counts
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: simulated word frequencies against rank on log-log axes, with a straight fitted line showing Zipf's law. Right: a dispersion plot with corpus position on the x-axis and three words on the y-axis; one word is clustered in the middle, the others are spread out."
set.seed(1252)
zipf_data <- tibble(
  rank = 1:300,
  frequency = 1e6 * rank^(-1.05) * exp(rnorm(300, 0, 0.15))
)

p_zipf <- ggplot(zipf_data, aes(rank, frequency)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = uzk_blue, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Zipf: log–log", x = "Rank", y = "Frequency")

dispersion <- tibble(
  word = rep(c("the", "prominence", "um"), c(220, 40, 90)),
  position = c(runif(220, 0, 5000), rnorm(40, 2500, 350), runif(90, 0, 5000))
)

p_disp <- ggplot(dispersion, aes(position, word, colour = word)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.6,
             position = position_jitter(height = 0.12, seed = 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma_format()) +
  labs(title = "Lexical dispersion", x = "Corpus position (tokens)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_zipf | p_disp
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Frequencies span orders of magnitude: **log–log** axes turn Zipf's law into a line and keep rare words visible.
- A straight line on log–log axes is a description, not a law; fit it and say so.
- Counts have no upper bound, so bars of raw counts invite wrong comparisons across corpora.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Frequency alone hides **clustering**: a word can be frequent but concentrated in one register or speaker.
- Dispersion plots put occurrences in corpus order; x is position, y is the word.
- Report both frequency and dispersion when the claim is about typicality.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Simulated: one word is clustered around the middle of the corpus, the other two are spread out. A frequency table would treat the clustered word as representative; the dispersion plot shows it is not. Mention `position_jitter(height = ...)` to separate overlapping occurrences without moving the corpus position.
:::

## Part IV: Models and data care {.center}

### After this part: report the model, protect the data

---

## Coefficient plots {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-coefficients
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "A coefficient plot for a linear model of F0 peak. Contrast and focus conditions have large positive effects with intervals far from zero; male sex and faster speech rate have negative effects; every interval is drawn with a zero reference line."
fit_f0 <- lm(f0_peak ~ condition + sex + speech_rate, data = prominence)
coef_f0 <- tidy(fit_f0, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(term = recode(term,
    "conditionfocus"    = "condition: focus",
    "conditioncontrast" = "condition: contrast",
    "sexmale"           = "sex: male",
    "speech_rate"       = "speech rate (syll/s)"
  ))

ggplot(coef_f0, aes(estimate, reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  colour = uzk_blue, size = 0.45) +
  labs(title = "The table, as a picture",
       subtitle = "lm(f0_peak ~ condition + sex + speech_rate)",
       x = "Effect on F0 peak (Hz)", y = NULL)
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- A coefficient plot is a forest plot for one model: estimates on the x-axis, terms on the y-axis, intervals and a zero line.
- Order terms by size; readers compare lengths, which is the most accurate encoding.
- Keep the units in the axis label; a coefficient without units is unreadable.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- For interactions, a coefficient plot is not enough; plot predictions or slopes (advanced deck).
- For models on a link scale, say whether the axis is log-odds, probability, or the response.
- The same layout serves `broom`, `modelsummary`, and posterior draws.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
A coefficient table is a list of numbers; the plot makes the comparison of magnitudes immediate. Note the units: condition effects are offsets in Hz relative to the plain condition, sex is an offset in Hz relative to female speakers, and speech rate is Hz per syllable per second. Mixing units on one axis is acceptable here only because all four are Hz; if you add a duration coefficient in milliseconds, split the figure or use facets. For interaction models, switch to predictions.
:::

---

## Posterior distributions {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-posterior
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Three posterior densities from simulated draws: a focus effect centred at 8 Hz, a speaker standard deviation near 12, and an item standard deviation near 6. Each density carries a bar marking the 95 percent credible interval."
set.seed(1252)
posterior <- tibble(
  parameter = factor(
    rep(c("focus effect (Hz)", "speaker SD (Hz)", "item SD (Hz)"), each = 4000),
    levels = c("focus effect (Hz)", "speaker SD (Hz)", "item SD (Hz)")
  ),
  draw = c(rnorm(4000, 8, 2.5), abs(rnorm(4000, 12, 2)), abs(rnorm(4000, 6, 1.5)))
)
posterior_summary <- posterior |>
  group_by(parameter) |>
  summarise(m = mean(draw), lo = quantile(draw, 0.025), hi = quantile(draw, 0.975),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(posterior, aes(draw)) +
  geom_density(fill = uzk_blue, alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_segment(data = posterior_summary,
               aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = 0, yend = 0),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ parameter, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "The whole estimate, not a point",
       subtitle = "simulated draws; the bar is the 95% credible interval",
       x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- A posterior is a distribution; a point estimate and an interval are summaries of it.
- Densities show skew and multimodality that an interval hides.
- `ggdist` provides half-eye, ridgeline, and dot-interval geoms for this; the hand-built version needs no extra package.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- For a decision, shade a **ROPE** and report the mass inside it.
- Mixed-model variance components (speaker SD, item SD) deserve a plot too; they are often the story.
- Say whether the draws are from a model, a bootstrap, or a simulation.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Simulated draws. The focus effect is well away from zero; the item SD is small, which says the effect generalises across items better than across speakers. Plotting variance components is uncommon and therefore informative. Mention `ggdist` and `brms::posterior_predict` for real workflows.
:::

## IPA, scripts, and fonts {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-ipa-fonts
#| fig-width: 10.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: a simulated vowel space with IPA labels i, small capital I, epsilon, ash, script a, and upsilon, all rendering correctly. Right: a grid of 16 IPA symbols by two fonts, showing that Albert Sans lacks 13 of the 16 glyphs while DejaVu Sans has all of them."
# The deck's own font, and a font with full IPA coverage.
ipa_symbols <- c("\u026a", "\u025b", "\u00e6", "\u0251", "\u0254", "\u028a",
                 "\u0283", "\u0292", "\u03b8", "\u00f0", "\u014b", "\u0294",
                 "\u027e", "\u02b0", "\u02e5", "\u02e9")

# glyph_info() returns index 0 for a codepoint the font file does not contain.
coverage <- tibble(symbol = ipa_symbols) |>
  mutate(
    albert = systemfonts::glyph_info(symbol, family = "Albert Sans", size = 12)$index > 0,
    dejavu = systemfonts::glyph_info(symbol, family = "DejaVu Sans", size = 12)$index > 0
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(albert, dejavu), names_to = "font", values_to = "present") |>
  mutate(
    font = recode(font, albert = "Albert Sans", dejavu = "DejaVu Sans"),
    font = factor(font, levels = c("DejaVu Sans", "Albert Sans")),
    symbol = factor(symbol, levels = ipa_symbols)
  )

n_missing <- sum(!coverage$present[coverage$font == "Albert Sans"])

p_coverage <- ggplot(coverage, aes(symbol, font, fill = present)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(present, "\u2713", "\u2717")), size = 4.2,
            colour = "white", family = "DejaVu Sans") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = uzk_turquoise, `FALSE` = uzk_coral), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(title = "What the font file contains",
       subtitle = sprintf("Albert Sans is missing %d of %d IPA glyphs", n_missing, length(ipa_symbols)),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x.top = element_text(size = rel(1.0)),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.9)))

# The same vowel space as before, now labelled in IPA.
set.seed(1252)
vowel_centres_ipa <- data.frame(
  vowel = c("\u0069", "\u026a", "\u025b", "\u00e6", "\u0251", "\u028a"),
  F1 = c(280, 400, 550, 700, 750, 320),
  F2 = c(2300, 2000, 1900, 1700, 1100, 900)
)
speaker_f1_ipa <- rnorm(8, 0, 25)
speaker_f2_ipa <- rnorm(8, 0, 70)

sim_vowels_ipa <- expand.grid(
  speaker = factor(1:8),
  vowel = vowel_centres_ipa$vowel,
  token = 1:25
) |>
  left_join(vowel_centres_ipa, by = "vowel") |>
  mutate(
    s = as.integer(speaker),
    F1 = F1 + speaker_f1_ipa[s] + rnorm(n(), 0, 30),
    F2 = F2 + speaker_f2_ipa[s] + rnorm(n(), 0, 80)
  )

vowel_labels <- sim_vowels_ipa |>
  group_by(vowel) |>
  summarise(F1 = mean(F1), F2 = mean(F2), .groups = "drop")

p_ipa_labels <- ggplot(sim_vowels_ipa, aes(F2, F1)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = vowel), alpha = 0.22, size = 0.6) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = vowel), level = 0.68, linewidth = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_label(data = vowel_labels, aes(label = vowel), family = "Albert Sans",
             size = 5.2, colour = uzk_blue, fill = "white",
             label.padding = unit(0.1, "lines")) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "What you see", subtitle = "the labels render anyway",
       x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)")

p_ipa_labels | p_coverage
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- IPA, combining diacritics, tone letters, and non-Latin scripts depend on the **font**, not on R.
- `ragg` **falls back silently**: the left panel looks right because the missing glyphs come from another font. The figure is fine; the typography is not.
- Check coverage with `systemfonts::glyph_info()`; an index of `0` means the glyph is absent.
- For PDF, embed fonts (`cairo_pdf`, `svglite`) or the glyphs will be substituted.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- Pick a font with wide coverage: DejaVu Sans, Noto Sans, Charis SIL, Doulos SIL.
- Set the family per layer when scripts differ: `geom_text(family = "Noto Sans")`.
- Put IPA in **labels and alt text**, not only in the legend.
- If a glyph still fails, spell it out in the caption.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Test on the target
Render the actual PDF or PNG and open it on the machine you will present from. The viewer lies.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The point of the figure is the mismatch. Albert Sans is the deck's own font and it lacks 13 of these 16 IPA glyphs, yet the left panel renders perfectly because ragg substitutes from a fallback font. So "it looks fine on my machine" is not evidence. `systemfonts::glyph_info()` returns the glyph index; 0 means the codepoint is not in the file. Ask the room to run it on their own house font. The fallback is not guaranteed on another machine, and in a PDF the substitution is baked in or the glyph is dropped. For journals, embed fonts or convert text to outlines. The advanced deck covers export; this is the linguistic special case.
:::

## Small N and disclosure {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-smalln
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left, labelled points for six simulated participants, each identified by a code; right, the same scores as anonymised points with a mean and 95 percent confidence interval. The left panel would allow re-identification; the right does not."
set.seed(1252)
small_data <- tibble(
  participant = sprintf("P%02d", 1:6),
  score = rnorm(6, 50, 10)
)
p_identified <- ggplot(small_data, aes(score, participant)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = uzk_coral) +
  labs(title = "Identifiable", subtitle = "codes + exact values", x = "Score", y = NULL)
p_anonymous <- ggplot(small_data, aes(1, score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0, size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7, colour = uzk_blue) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.8, 1.2)) +
  labs(title = "Disclosed", subtitle = "aggregate + interval", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_identified | p_anonymous
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Participant codes, exact dates, and rare combinations can re-identify people, especially in small samples.
- Do not put raw IDs, session dates, or free-text responses in figures.
- Suppress small cells; report aggregates with *n*.
- Audio examples need consent for **sharing**, not only for collection.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- Keep the analysis reproducible with pseudonymous keys stored separately.
- For qualitative examples, quote with permission and remove identifying details.
- Check your ethics approval and the CRC's data policy; when in doubt, aggregate.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Small N is the norm in experimental linguistics. A plot with participant codes and exact scores is often enough to identify a colleague's child or a clinical participant. The right panel keeps the distribution and the interval but drops the identifiers. The SFB's data and sustainability project has guidance; point people there rather than improvising.
:::

## Missing data and exclusions {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-missing
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: a tile grid of missingness by item and condition, showing that the focus condition loses more trials. Right: a density of reaction times on a log axis with a dashed line at the 95th percentile marking a possible exclusion threshold."
set.seed(1252)
trial_data <- expand.grid(
  participant = factor(1:40),
  item = factor(sprintf("I%02d", 1:20)),
  condition = c("plain", "focus")
) |>
  mutate(
    drop = rbinom(n(), 1, ifelse(condition == "focus", 0.25, 0.10)),
    rt = rlnorm(n(), log(600), 0.35)
  )

missing_item <- trial_data |>
  group_by(condition, item) |>
  summarise(p_missing = mean(drop), .groups = "drop")

p_missing <- ggplot(missing_item, aes(item, condition, fill = p_missing)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), option = "C",
                       breaks = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4),
                       guide = guide_colourbar(barwidth = unit(5, "cm"))) +
  labs(title = "Missingness by item", subtitle = "simulated", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       fill = "Missing") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.7)))

p_rt <- ggplot(trial_data, aes(rt)) +
  geom_density(fill = uzk_blue, alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(trial_data$rt, 0.95),
             linetype = 2, colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Reaction times", subtitle = "where would you cut?",
       x = "RT (ms, log scale)", y = NULL)

p_missing | p_rt
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Show **where** data are missing, not only how much: a condition that loses trials changes the estimate.
- Report *n* per cell and the exclusion rule; a symmetry assumption is a claim.
- Compare results with and without exclusions (sensitivity), and say so.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Show the distribution before cutting outliers; a density with a threshold is honest.
- RTs are skewed: log axes and medians, not means of raw milliseconds.
- Never drop "outliers" silently; the figure should make the rule visible.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Simulated: the focus condition loses about 25% of trials, so a naïve comparison of condition means is biased. The tile grid shows the pattern; the RT density shows where a cut would fall. Ask the room where they would draw the line and what they would report. The advanced deck's interval and model slides cover the estimation side.
:::

---

## Five takeaways {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
1. **Match the figure to the data shape.** Time within trial, formants per token, ordinal ratings, and corpus positions each need their own idiom.
2. **Show individuals.** Every-speaker lines, caterpillars, and per-unit effects prevent over-generalising from a mean.
3. **Distributions beat means** for ratings and proportions; intervals must respect bounds and design.
4. **Plot the model.** Coefficients and posteriors are more informative than tables, and variance components are part of the story.
5. **The output is part of the analysis.** Fonts, disclosure, missingness, and exclusions are scientific choices, not formatting.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-important}
### The grammar travels

The same `ggplot2` grammar covers all of this. What changes is the data shape and the question — not the layers, scales, or facets you already know.
:::

**Next steps**

- Re-plot one figure from your own project using the shape of its data.
- Try a difference curve, a caterpillar plot, or a coefficient plot this week.
- Check one figure for font coverage and disclosure before the next talk.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Close by mapping the five points onto the four parts. The common thread is that the grammar is fixed; the domain supplies the data shapes. If the room is mixed, ask each person to name their data shape and the idiom that fits it.
:::

## Extensions: distributions and labels {.smaller}

Most of what this deck builds by hand has a maintained extension. Install only what you need: every package is a dependency you have to keep working.

| Package | What it adds | Where it helps in prominence work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`ggdist`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggdist) | Half-eye, dot, and gradient intervals; ROPE shading | Posterior draws, per-speaker effects, anything with a distribution |
| [`ggridges`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggridges) | Ridgeline densities | F0 or duration distributions per speaker, stacked and comparable |
| [`ggbeeswarm`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggbeeswarm) | Quasirandom and swarm jitter | Ratings and accuracy with few observations per cell |
| [`ggrepel`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggrepel) | Labels that push away from each other | Vowel labels, speaker IDs, item names |
| [`ggtext`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggtext) | Markdown and HTML in labels | *Italics*, F~0~, IPA, coloured words in titles |
| [`ggpmisc`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggpmisc) | Equations, tables, and annotations as layers | Model equations and small tables inside a panel |
| [`ggfittext`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggfittext) | Text that shrinks to fit its box | Labels inside bars and tiles |

::: {.callout-tip}
### Start with two

`ggdist` and `ggtext` cover most of what this deck builds by hand. Add `ggbeeswarm` if your cells are small, and `ggrepel` the first time two vowel labels collide.
:::

::: {.notes}
`ggdist` is the one to install first if you work with Bayesian models; it replaces most hand-built interval code. `ggtext` matters for linguistics specifically: it is the practical way to get italics, subscripts, and IPA into a title without pasting plotmath expressions. `ggbeeswarm` solves the ratings problem from Part III when each cell has only a handful of observations.
:::

---

## Extensions: layout, categories, colour {.smaller}

| Package | What it adds | Where it helps in prominence work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`ggforce`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggforce) | `facet_zoom()`, `geom_mark_ellipse()`, `geom_sina()` | Zoom into a crowded vowel region without changing the scale |
| [`ggnewscale`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggnewscale) | A second colour or fill scale in one plot | Points coloured by vowel plus tiles shaded by probability |
| [`ggalluvial`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggalluvial) | Alluvial and Sankey flows | How annotation categories change across turns or raters |
| [`ggmosaic`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggmosaic) | Mosaic plots | Two categorical variables, e.g. condition × response category |
| [`ggseqplot`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggseqplot) | Sequence plots, built on `TraMineR` | Gaze, gesture phase, or annotation state over time |
| [`ggupset`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggupset) | UpSet plots | Which participants or items fall in which condition sets |
| [`ggbreak`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggbreak) | Axis breaks | A gap you must show — label it, or use a facet instead |
| [`scico`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=scico) | Scientific, perceptually uniform palettes | Sequential and diverging scales that survive a projector |
| [`ggokabeito`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggokabeito) | Okabe–Ito colour-blind-safe palette | Categorical scales for talks and print |

::: {.callout-warning}
### Two to treat with care

`ggbreak` hides part of the axis; a reader who skips the label will misread the figure. `ggalluvial` and `ggseqplot` are excellent but assume a data shape (one row per transition or per time point) that most acoustic data frames do not have yet — reshape first, then plot.
:::

::: {.notes}
`ggforce::facet_zoom()` is the honest alternative to truncating an axis: it keeps the full range visible and adds a magnified panel. `ggnewscale` is what you reach for when one plot needs two colour meanings. `ggbreak` is listed with a warning — a broken axis is easy to misread, so prefer a facet or a log scale, and if you must break, label the break.
:::

---

## Domain packages, and how to choose {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Acoustic and phonetic

- [`phonR`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=phonR) — Lobanov and other normalisations, vowel plotting helpers
- [`vowels`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=vowels) — reference vowel data and normalisation methods
- [`wrassp`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=wrassp) — F0, formants, and intensity from the ASSP library
- [`emuR`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=emuR) — query and plot from speech databases
- [`praatpicture`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=praatpicture) — Praat-style annotation plots built on ggplot2

### Corpus and text

- [`quanteda`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=quanteda) — corpus statistics that feed the plots
- [`tidytext`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tidytext) — token and frequency tables in tidy shape
- [`lingtypology`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=lingtypology) — typological features and maps

The next two slides run `phonR`, `vowels`, `quanteda`, and `tidytext` on real data.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### How to choose an extension

- **Does it still build?** Check the CRAN checks page and the last release date before you depend on it in a paper.
- **Does it compose with the grammar?** A geom or scale you can place in a pipeline is safer than a function that returns a finished picture.
- **Can you read the source?** Most extensions are a few hundred lines; the ones that are not are the ones that surprise you.
- **Prefer the layer you understand.** A hand-built `geom_segment()` you can explain beats a helper you cannot.
- **For a paper, fewer dependencies.** Reproducibility is easier when the figure needs three packages, not thirteen.

::: {.callout-tip}
### The rule of thumb

If the extension saves you a paragraph of explanation in the methods section, keep it. If it hides a choice you would have to defend, build the layer yourself.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The domain packages are not ggplot2 extensions; they produce the data frame that ggplot2 draws. That separation is the point: `wrassp` or `emuR` gives you F0 tracks, `phonR` normalises them, and the plotting grammar is unchanged. On choosing: the failure mode in published work is a figure that cannot be rebuilt because a helper package changed its defaults. Ask the room which packages they already use and whether the figures still render.
:::

---

## In practice: acoustic data {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-domain-acoustic
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of the same 426 vowel tokens from two speakers in the ohiovowels data. Left: raw F1 and F2 in Hz, where the two speakers form separate vertical bands. Right: the same tokens after Lobanov normalisation with phonR, where the two speakers overlap and the vowel space is shared."
# Real data: 2 speakers, 24 vowel classes, 426 tokens (vowels::ohiovowels).
# Keep only speaker-by-vowel cells with at least 5 tokens; a single token has
# no standard deviation, and normLobanov() returns NaN for it.
ohio <- ohiovowels |>
  select(speaker, vowel.frame, F1, F2) |>
  group_by(speaker, vowel.frame) |>
  filter(n() >= 5) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(vowel.frame = droplevels(vowel.frame))

# phonR does the normalisation; the output is a plain data frame, so ggplot2
# draws it exactly as before. This is the whole point of the separation.
ohio_norm <- ohio |>
  group_by(speaker) |>
  group_modify(~ as_tibble(normLobanov(.x[, c("F1", "F2")], group = .x$vowel.frame))) |>
  ungroup()

speaker_cols <- c(JOHG09 = uzk_blue, OHDMTV_M = uzk_coral)

p_raw <- ggplot(ohio, aes(F2, F1, colour = speaker)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.9) +
  scale_x_reverse() + scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = speaker_cols) +
  labs(title = "Raw Hz", subtitle = "two speakers, two bands",
       x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = NULL)

p_norm <- ggplot(ohio_norm, aes(F2, F1, colour = speaker)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.9) +
  scale_x_reverse() + scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = speaker_cols) +
  labs(title = "Lobanov, via phonR", subtitle = "one shared space",
       x = "F2 (z)", y = "F1 (z)", colour = NULL)

p_raw | p_norm
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- `vowels::ohiovowels` is real data: 2 speakers, 24 vowel classes, 426 tokens after filtering.
- Raw speaker means differ by **105 Hz in F1** and **340 Hz in F2**; after Lobanov both are exactly 0.
- `phonR::normLobanov()` returns a plain data frame, so the plotting grammar does not change.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
- `phonR::vowelMeansPolygonArea()` gives vowel-space area: 146,000 vs 74,000 Hz² here — a size difference, not a vowel difference.
- Filter before you normalise: a cell with one token has no SD, and the function returns `NaN` rather than warning.
- `vowels::vowelplot()` is the package's own base-graphics plot; use it to check, then rebuild in ggplot2.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This is the normalisation claim from the vowel-space slide, now with real data and a real package. The left panel is the problem: the two speakers occupy separate vertical bands, so a reader sees speaker, not vowel. The right panel is the same tokens after Lobanov. Note that the normalisation is per speaker and uses each speaker's own mean and SD, which is why both speaker means become exactly zero. The NaN is a genuine trap: `normLobanov()` divides by the SD of the group, and a group of one has no SD, so you get NaN silently. Filter first. The polygon area is the other phonR function worth knowing; it turns "this speaker has a bigger vowel space" into a number you can plot.
:::

---

## In practice: corpus data {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-domain-corpus
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Two panels from the US presidential inaugural addresses. Left: the frequency of five words per 10,000 words against year, as points with a smooth trend line; nation and freedom rise, people stays flat. Right: the seven most frequent content words for Democratic and Republican speeches as horizontal bars."
# quanteda builds the document-feature matrix; ggplot2 draws it.
inaug_tokens <- tokens(data_corpus_inaugural, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE)
inaug_full   <- dfm(inaug_tokens)
inaug_sel    <- dfm_select(inaug_full, pattern = c("freedom", "liberty", "nation", "people", "power"))

inaug_counts <- convert(inaug_sel, to = "data.frame") |>
  select(-doc_id) |>
  mutate(Year = docvars(data_corpus_inaugural)$Year,
         total = ntoken(inaug_full)) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Year, total), names_to = "word", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(per10k = n / total * 1e4)

p_time <- ggplot(inaug_counts, aes(Year, per10k, colour = word)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
              se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Frequency over time", subtitle = "quanteda",
       x = NULL, y = "Per 10k words", colour = NULL)

# tidytext: one row per token, which is the shape most dplyr verbs expect.
inaug_tidy <- convert(data_corpus_inaugural, to = "data.frame") |>
  select(doc_id, text, Party) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(), by = "word")

inaug_top <- inaug_tidy |>
  filter(Party %in% c("Democratic", "Republican")) |>
  count(Party, word, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(Party) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 7) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, n, Party))

p_party <- ggplot(inaug_top, aes(n, word, fill = Party)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Party, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Democratic = uzk_blue, Republican = uzk_coral)) +
  labs(title = "Top words by party", subtitle = "tidytext",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.8)))

p_time | p_party
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- `quanteda` gives a document-feature matrix; `convert()` turns it into a data frame that ggplot2 can draw.
- Divide by **document length** (`ntoken()`), not by the count of the words you selected — the first version of this figure did the latter and produced nonsense.
- `tidytext::unnest_tokens()` gives one row per token, the shape `dplyr` verbs expect.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
- `reorder_within()` + `scale_y_reordered()` are what make per-facet ordering work; without them both facets share one order.
- `anti_join(get_stopwords())` is a one-line stop-word filter that keeps the pipeline readable.
- Both packages stop at the data frame. The grammar, the theme, and the honesty rules are unchanged.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Two packages, one grammar. `quanteda` is the right tool when you want a document-feature matrix and the operations that go with it: selecting features, weighting, and per-document counts. `tidytext` is the right tool when you want one row per token so that ordinary `dplyr` verbs work. They compose: convert the corpus once and use both. The denominator mistake is worth dwelling on, because it is the most common error in corpus frequency plots: if you divide by the sum of the words you selected, every line is a share of a handful of words and the axis means nothing. Use the document length. The `reorder_within()` point is small but it is the difference between a readable faceted bar chart and a wrong one.
:::

## Further reading {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Time, space, and models

- [ggplot2 book](https://ggplot2-book.org/) chapters on layers and scales [@wickham2024ggplot2]
- Wood, *Generalized Additive Models* — for contour smooths [@wood2017gam]
- [`mgcv`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mgcv) and [`gratia`](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/) for GAMM plots
- [`ggdist`](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/) for posterior and uncertainty geoms [@kay2024ggdist]
- [`marginaleffects`](https://marginaleffects.com/) for predictions and slopes
- [ggplot2 extension gallery](https://exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org/gallery/) — browse by geom, scale, or task
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Linguistics and data care

- [`phonTools`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=phonTools) and [`praatpicture`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=praatpicture) for acoustic data in R
- [`naniar`](https://naniar.njtierney.com/) for missing-data visualisation
- [`viridis`](https://sjmgarnier.github.io/viridis/) and [ColorBrewer](https://colorbrewer2.org/) for palettes
- [`reprex`](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/) for asking questions with a reproducible example
:::
